# Why Not Just Regression? {background-color="#40666e"}

## The Trouble with a Straight Line {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
set.seed(4711)
n  <- 300
x1 <- runif(n, 0, 10); x2 <- runif(n, 0, 10)
# a threshold effect in x1 whose size depends on x2 -- an interaction
y  <- ifelse(x1 < 5, 10, 25) + ifelse(x2 > 6, 12, 0) + rnorm(n, 0, 2)
d  <- tibble(x1, x2, y, fit = fitted(lm(y ~ x1 + x2)))
ggplot(d, aes(fit, y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, colour = "#31688EFF") +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Fitted by OLS", y = "Observed",
       title = paste0("Linear model, R2 = ",
                      round(summary(lm(y ~ x1 + x2))$r.squared, 2))) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
The data were generated by a rule a child could state:

> *If* $X_1 < 5$ the score is low. And if on top of that $X_2 > 6$, add
> a bonus.

A linear model in $X_1$ and $X_2$ cannot express it. To recover it we
would have to know **in advance** to add:

- a threshold at $X_1 = 5$,
- a threshold at $X_2 = 6$,
- and the interaction between them.
:::
:::::

## What We Actually Want

- Real relationships are often **non-linear**---effects that switch on
  at a threshold rather than accumulating smoothly.
- And they are often **conditional**: the effect of one feature depends
  on the value of another.
- In a regression we must *specify* these in advance: every polynomial
  term, every knot, every interaction. With $P$ features there are
  $\binom{P}{2}$ two-way interactions alone, before we consider
  three-way ones or non-linearity.
- In social science we rarely have theory sharp enough to say which of
  them matter.

::: callout-important
## The ambition for today

An algorithm that finds the thresholds and the interactions **from the
data**, without being told where to look.
:::

## Greedy Algorithms Can Deliver

- The trick is to stop trying to write down the whole function at once.
- Instead, ask a much smaller question, over and over: *given where I
  am, what single cut of the data would help most right now?*
- Each cut is a threshold, so non-linearity is automatic.
- Each cut sits inside the region carved out by earlier cuts, so
  **interactions are automatic too**---a split on $X_2$ that happens
  only where $X_1 < 5$ is exactly a conditional effect.
- The good news: nobody has to specify anything. The structure is
  discovered.
- The price is that each decision is only *locally* optimal. That is
  what "greedy" means, and the rest of the afternoon is largely about
  managing the consequences.

# Greedy Learning {background-color="#40666e"}

## What Is a Tree?

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  A[X1 less<br>then 5]-->|No|B[Class 1]
  A-->|Yes|C[X2 less<br>then 2]
  C-->|No|D[Class 2]
  C-->|Yes|E[Class 3]
```

A [**tree**]{.alert} in tree-based learning is a flowchart-like
structure consisting of [**nodes**]{.alert} representing decisions or
splits on features, and [**leaves**]{.alert} that represent outcomes
(labels or scores).

## Trees and Rules

- A tree can also be expressed as a series of decision rules.
- For instance,
  $$\begin{align}
  & \text{IF} \ X_1 \geq  5 \ \text{THEN} \\
  & \hspace{1cm} C_1 \\
  &\text{ELSE IF} \ X_1 < 5 \ \text{AND} \ X_2 \geq 2 \ \text{THEN} \\
  & \hspace{1cm} C_2 \\
  &\text{ELSE} \\
  & \hspace{1cm} C_3 \\
  &\text{END IF}
  \end{align}$$
- For this reason, we also speak of rule-based algorithms.

## Decisions as Axis-Parallel Splits

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)

# Class regions based on decision rules
regions <- data.frame(
  xmin = c(0, 0, 5),
  xmax = c(5, 5, 10),
  ymin = c(0, 2, 0),  # Class 3 at bottom left, Class 2 above it, Class 1 right side
  ymax = c(2, 5, 5),
  label = factor(c("Class 3", "Class 2", "Class 1"), levels = c("Class 1", "Class 2", "Class 3"))
)

# Assign consistent colors (light blue, green, red)
region_colors <- c("Class 1" = "#D0E4F5",  # light blue
                   "Class 2" = "#D0F5D5",  # light green
                   "Class 3" = "#F5D0D0")  # light red

# Plot
ggplot() +
  geom_rect(data = regions, aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax, fill = label),
            color = NA, alpha = 0.6) +
  
  # Decision boundaries
  geom_vline(xintercept = 5, linetype = "solid", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = 5, y = 2, yend = 2), linetype = "solid", linewidth = 1) +
  
  # Region labels
  annotate("text", x = 7.5, y = 2.5, label = "Class 1", size = 5) +
  annotate("text", x = 2.5, y = 3.5, label = "Class 2", size = 5) +
  annotate("text", x = 2.5, y = 1, label = "Class 3", size = 5) +
  
  labs(x = expression(X[1]), y = expression(X[2])) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = region_colors, guide = "none") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 5)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
```

We make one split parallel to the $y$-axis and one split parallel to the
$x$-axis. The latter applies only for a certain range of values of
$X_1$.

## Greedy Learning

- The idea of considering each criterion in succession, possibly with
  repetition, renders the approach greedy.
- **Definition:**
  - Greedy algorithms seek to determine a global optimum by making a
    series of locally optimal decisions.
- Since we do not consider all features simultaneously, each decision is
  optimal only in a *local* sense.
- Nevertheless, these algorithms often perform well.
- An added benefit is that they can be interpreted with ease.

## Greediness Aplenty

- There are many greedy algorithms.
- We shall focus on CART.
- There are many others, however, including C5.0 [@quinlan1993C45],
  CHAID [@kass1980Exploratory], conditional inference forests
  [@hothorn2006Unbiased], ID3 [@quinlan1986Induction], OneR
  [@holte1993Very], and QUEST [@loh1997Split].
- In addition, there are numerous ensemble learners that follow a
  tree-based structure.

# Classification and Regression Trees {background-color="#40666e"}

## An All-Purpose Algorithm

- @breiman1984Classification developed the [**classification and
  regression trees**]{.alert} (CART) algorithm, which can handle both
  classification and regression tasks.
- It generates an easily interpretable set of results.
- Moreover, it has an automatic facility for handling missing data.

## Example of a Regression Task

```{r}
#| message: false
# Load necessary libraries
library(MASS)
library(viridis)  # for color-blind-friendly color scales

# Set seed for reproducibility
set.seed(3841)

# Define means and covariance matrix for two distributions
mu_group1 <- c(3, 5)
mu_group2 <- c(7, 5)
Sigma <- 0.5 * diag(2)

# Generate multivariate normal data for two groups
group1 <- mvrnorm(50, mu_group1, Sigma)
group2 <- mvrnorm(50, mu_group2, Sigma)

# Combine both groups into a single data frame
data <- rbind.data.frame(group1, group2)

# Add a random error term
data$error <- rnorm(100, mean = 0, sd = 1)

# Define the response variable: a step function on x1
data$y <- ifelse(data$V1 < 5, 100 + data$error, 200 + data$error)

# Prepare data for plotting
plot_df <- data %>%
  transmute(
    x1 = V1,
    x2 = V2,
    y = y
  )

# Create the scatter plot
ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = x1, y = x2, color = y)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_color_viridis(option = "D", direction = -1, name = "Response y") +
  labs(
    title = "Scatter Plot of Simulated Data",
    subtitle = "Color indicates response variable y",
    x = "X1",
    y = "X2"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 15) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "right"
  )

```

## Objective

- We want to make a series of axis parallel splits that improve the
  purity of the resulting nodes.
- As in other greedy algorithms, we do this by considering one feature
  at a time.
- We continue the process until we can no longer improve node purity.

## Node Purity for Numeric Labels

- With numeric scores, we want partitions that hold homogeneous values.
- Thus, we want to reduce the standard deviation in each partition.
- Let
  $$\sigma = \sum_j w_j \sigma_j$$
  be the total dispersion, where (1) $\sigma_j$ is the standard
  deviation in partition or node and (2) $w_j$ is the proportion of
  instances within the partition.

## Information Gain

- We seek to improve on the total dispersion, i.e., we maximize the
  standard deviation reduction
  $$\text{SDR} = \sigma_0 - \sigma_1$$
  where (1) $\sigma_0$ is the total dispersion ex ante and (2)
  $\sigma_1$ is the total dispersion ex post
- Features and values of those features are selected to optimize SDR.

## Illustration

```{r}
ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = x1, y = x2, color = y)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_color_viridis(
    option = "C", 
    direction = -1, 
    name = "Response y",
    guide = guide_colorbar(barwidth = 1.5, barheight = 10)
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 5,
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 1,
    color = "gray40"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Scatter Plot of Simulated Data",
    subtitle = "Vertical line shows decision threshold at X1 = 5",
    x = "X1",
    y = "X2"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 15) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "right",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

```

\(1\) $\sigma_0 = 50.243$. (2) In the West-partition, $\sigma_W = 0.933$
and $w_W = 0.5$; in the East-partition, $\sigma_E = 0.913$ and
$w_E = 0.5 \Rightarrow \sigma_1 = 0.924$. (3) SDR = 41.320.

## How CART Chooses a Feature and a Cut-Point {.smaller}

At every node, CART searches *exhaustively*: every feature, every
possible cut-point.

``` {.default code-line-numbers="|5|6|7|8|9-10|11|12|13|17"}
FUNCTION BestSplit(S):

    best ← (feature: none, point: none, gain: 0)

    FOR EACH feature X_p DO
        v(1) < v(2) < ... < v(K)  ←  sorted unique values of X_p in S
        FOR k = 1 TO K - 1 DO
            c   ← ( v(k) + v(k+1) ) / 2          # candidate cut-point
            S_L ← { i ∈ S : x_ip ≤ c }
            S_R ← { i ∈ S : x_ip >  c }
            IF min(|S_L|, |S_R|) < min_n THEN skip to next k
            gain ← I(S) − [ w_L · I(S_L) + w_R · I(S_R) ]
            IF gain > best.gain THEN best ← (X_p, c, gain)
        END FOR
    END FOR

    RETURN best
```

::: {style="font-size: 80%"}
$I(\cdot)$ is the impurity measure: $\sigma$ (or the within-node sum of
squares) for regression, Gini or entropy for classification.
$w_L = \lvert S_L \rvert / \lvert S \rvert$. Note the split is always
**binary**.
:::

## Growing the Tree {.smaller}

`BestSplit` handles one node. The tree is built by recursion.

``` {.default code-line-numbers="|3-5|7|9|11-14|17-18"}
FUNCTION Grow(S, d):

    IF d = max_depth OR |S| < min_split OR S is pure THEN
        RETURN Leaf( mean of y in S     # regression
                     majority class     # classification )

    (X*, c*, gain*) ← BestSplit(S)

    IF gain* ≤ 0 THEN RETURN Leaf( ... )      # no split improves purity

    RETURN Node(
        split : X* ≤ c* ,
        left  : Grow( { i ∈ S : x_iX* ≤ c* }, d + 1 ),
        right : Grow( { i ∈ S : x_iX* >  c* }, d + 1 )
    )

T_max ← Grow(training set, d = 0)      # deliberately grow too far
T*    ← Prune(T_max, α)                # then cut back — see below
```

## Why the Search Is Feasible {.smaller}

- A numeric feature taking $n$ distinct values offers only $n-1$
  candidate cut-points, not infinitely many.
- Sorting once per feature and sweeping $c$ from left to right lets
  $I(S_L)$ and $I(S_R)$ be updated from running sums $\Rightarrow$ one
  pass per feature.
- Cost per node is therefore on the order of $P \cdot n \log n$ for $P$
  features.
- A categorical feature with $L$ levels has $2^{L-1} - 1$ possible
  binary splits. For regression and two-class problems,
  @breiman1984Classification show that ordering the levels by their mean
  response reduces this to just $L - 1$ splits to check.

::: notes
The exhaustive scan is what makes the algorithm greedy but not naive:
within a node it really does find the globally best single split. What
it cannot do is look ahead — a split that looks poor now might enable an
excellent pair of splits below it, and CART will never find it.
:::

## Decision Tree

```{r}
#| message: false
library(rpart)
library(rpart.plot)
data$X1 <- data$V1
data$X2 <- data$V2
cart.fit <- rpart(y ~ X1 + X2,
                  data = data,
                  method = "anova",
                  control = rpart.control(cp = 0.00001))
prp(cart.fit)
```

## Prediction

- Imagine we receive a query with values $(x_{i1},x_{i2})$.
- We decide in which partition of the feature space the query is
  located.
- We then allocate the corresponding mean, $\mu_j$.

## Pruning

- As in all greedy algorithms, over-fitting the CART is a concern.
- @breiman1984Classification introduce a complexity parameter to
  regularize the fit:
  $$R_{\alpha}(T) = \text{RE}(T) + \alpha \lvert T \rvert$$
  where (1) $T$ is the tree; (2) $R$ is the risk (i.e., expected
  loss); (3) RE is the resubstitution error; and (4) $\lvert T \rvert$
  is the size of the tree, i.e., the number of terminal nodes/leaves
- We often treat the complexity parameter $\alpha \geq 0$ as a tuning
  parameter.
- Sometimes, other tuning parameters are available as well: (1) the
  maximum tree depth and (2) the minimum node size at the leaves.

## Our Data for the Afternoon

:::: panel-tabset
### The Problem

- We continue with the Boston Housing data [@harrison1978Hedonic].
- As before, the target is `cmedv`, a **numeric score**.
- We use the full set of features, including demographics, geography,
  and policy-relevant variables: pollution, schooling, crime, and taxes.
- You met these data in the regularization lecture. This afternoon we
  ask what a linear model could not: where are the thresholds, and which
  features interact?

### Setup

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
library(mlbench)
library(tidymodels)
library(tidyverse)
tidymodels_prefer()

data("BostonHousing2")
boston <- BostonHousing2 |>
  mutate(chas = as.numeric(chas) - 1) |>
  select(-town, -tract, -lon, -lat, -medv)

set.seed(821)
boston_split <- initial_split(boston, prop = 0.8, strata = cmedv)
train_data   <- training(boston_split)
test_data    <- testing(boston_split)
```

### Note

::: callout-important
One split, set once, reused by **every** algorithm today. That is what
makes the scoreboard honest --- the same training rows and the same
held-out rows throughout.
:::
::::

## CART on the Boston Data

::: panel-tabset
### Recipe and Model

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
cart_recipe <- recipe(cmedv ~ ., data = train_data)

cart_spec <- decision_tree(
    tree_depth      = tune(),
    min_n           = tune(),
    cost_complexity = tune()
  ) |>
  set_mode("regression") |>
  set_engine("rpart")

cart_flow <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(cart_recipe) |>
  add_model(cart_spec)
```

### Tuning

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
cart_param <- extract_parameter_set_dials(cart_spec)
set.seed(5161)
cart_grid <- grid_space_filling(cart_param, size = 20,
                                type = "latin_hypercube")
set.seed(1923)
cv_folds <- vfold_cv(train_data, v = 5)

library(future)
plan(multisession)
cart_tune <- cart_flow |>
  tune_grid(cv_folds, grid = cart_grid,
            metrics = metric_set(rmse, rsq))
cart_best <- select_best(cart_tune, metric = "rmse")
cart_best
plan(sequential)
```

### Final Fit

```{r}
#| echo: true
cart_final <- cart_flow |>
  finalize_workflow(cart_best) |>
  fit(data = train_data)
```

### The Tree

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
library(rpart.plot)
rpart.plot(extract_fit_engine(cart_final))
```

### Performance

```{r}
#| echo: true
cart_final |>
  predict(test_data) |>
  bind_cols(test_data) |>
  metrics(truth = cmedv, estimate = .pred)
```
:::

## About the Re-sampling

`v = 5` with no repeats is a **teaching compromise** --- it keeps every
model in this block inside class time. For real development work use
`v = 10` with `repeats = 5`: ten times the computation, but a far more
stable choice of hyper-parameters. More folds reduce *bias* in the
estimate; repeats reduce *noise* in the choice.

## CART for Classification

- For classification, we want the classes in each partition to be as
  homogenous as possible.
- One way to measure this is through **entropy**:
  $$\text{Ent} = - \sum_{i=1}^M \pi_i \log_2 \pi_i$$
  where $M$ denotes the number of classes.
- Alternatively, we can use the **Gini index**:
  $$\text{Gini} = 1 - \sum_{i=1}^M pi_i^2$$

# Overcoming the Limits of a Single Tree: Ensembles {background-color="#40666e"}

## The Limitations of CART

- Although CARTS have many advantages, including ease of interpretation,
  they also suffer from limitations.
- These include:
  - Susceptibility to over-fitting
  - High variance
  - Sensitivity to outliers and noise

## Ensembles of Predictions

::: callout-important
## Definition

Ensemble learners are algorithms that combine the predictions from two
or more models.
:::

- The overarching goal is to obtain better predictions.
- This can be done by reducing
  1.  Bias error (boosting)
  2.  Variance error (bagging)
- We can ensemble models of
  - The same type $\Rightarrow$ **homogeneous ensembles** (bagging and
    boosting)
  - Different types $\Rightarrow$ **heterogeneous ensembles**
    (stacking---not further discussed here)

## Base Learners

- Typically, we assemble [**base learners**]{.alert}:
  - Simple models (e.g. a split on one feature).
- We also speak of [**weak learners**]{.alert}:
  - Models that perform only slightly better than chance.
- We tend to prefer the use of base learners because
  - It simplifies computation.
  - Avoids over-fitting at each step.
  - It is unnecessary to fit complex models because ensemble methods are
    designed to ultimately give a good bias-variance trade-off.

## Parallel versus Sequential Approaches

- Parallel approaches entail fitting many models in parallel, i.e.,
  independently from each other.
  - Bagging
- Sequential approaches entail fitting models in sequence, rendering
  them contingent on each other.
  - Boosting

## Building Ensembles

- A key difference to what we have done so far is repeated fitting:
  - We build $R$ models instead of one, where $R$ is usually a sizable
    number.
- Because we end up with $R$ predictions, another key difference is that
  we need to combine them:
  - Use a simple or weighted average for regression tasks.
  - Use the mode for classification tasks (voting).
- Think of it as an orchestra: many players, each contributing a part,
  and the value is in the combination rather than in any one
  performance.

## What Is Bagging? {.smaller}

:::::: columns
:::: {.column width="50%"}
![](images/bagging.png){fig-align="center"}

::: {style="font-size: 75%"}
**Source:**
[Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bootstrap_aggregating)
:::
::::

::: {.column width="50%"}
- [**Bagging**]{.alert} = **B**ootstrap **Agg**regat**ing**, proposed by
  @breiman1996Bagging.

- Three steps:

  1.  Draw $R$ bootstrap re-samples from the training data.
  2.  Fit a learner in each re-sample.
  3.  Aggregate --- average for regression, vote for classification.

- The trees are fitted **in parallel** and never see each other. Nothing
  is sequential here.

- Averaging $R$ noisy-but-unbiased trees cuts variance without adding
  bias --- exactly the error CART suffers from.
:::
::::::

## OOB

- A bootstrap re-sample typically leaves out some instances—the
  [**out-of-bag**]{.alert} (OOB) set.
- We find all of the models not trained by an OOB instance.
- We then make a prediction for the OOB instance and compute the
  prediction (OOB) error.
- We average all of the OOB errors.

## What Is Boosting? {.smaller}

:::::: columns
:::: {.column width="52%"}
![](images/boosting.png){fig-align="center"}

::: {style="font-size: 75%"}
**Source:**
[Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boosting_(machine_learning))
:::
::::

::: {.column width="48%"}
- [**Boosting**]{.alert} is *sequential*: each learner is fitted to what
  its predecessors could not explain.
- Learners are deliberately **weak** --- often a stump. A single one is
  barely better than nothing; hundreds in sequence are formidable.
- Where bagging reduces **variance** by averaging independent trees,
  boosting reduces **bias** by correcting a running fit.
:::
::::::

## Two Families, and They Differ in What "Got Wrong" Means

1.  **Re-weighting** (AdaBoost): mis-predicted instances get larger
    weights, so the next learner tries harder on them
    [@freund1995DecisionTheoretic].
2.  **Gradient boosting** (GBM, XGBoost): the next learner is fitted
    directly to the *residual* --- the part of the target still
    unexplained [@friedman2001Greedy].

# Random Forests {background-color="#40666e"}

## Sampling Instances and Features I

- @breiman2001Random proposed random forests as an improvement over
  bagging.

- The central idea of bagging is to sample instances.

- Random forests add to that the idea of sampling features.

  - At **every node** of every tree, we draw a fresh random subset of
    features and search for the best split within that subset only
    [@breiman2001Random].
  - This is not once per tree: two sibling nodes in the same tree
    consider different candidate features.

- Thus, two elements of randomness are at play.

## Sampling Instances and Features II

- This reduces the risk that splits are made on the same features time
  and again:
  - There is less correlation between predictions.
  - Measures of feature importance become less biased.

## How Many Features?

- We sample $M < P$ features for each tree.
- One way to set $M$ is to follow a rule-of-thumb:
  - $M = \sqrt{P}$ for classification tasks.
  - $M =\frac{P}{3}$ for regression tasks.
- Alternatively and more commonly, we can set $M$ through
  cross-validation.

## How a Random Forest Is Grown {.smaller}

Two independent sources of randomness: the **rows** (bootstrap) and, at
every node, the **columns**.

``` {.default code-line-numbers="|4|5|6|8|11|13|15|17|19-21"}
FUNCTION RandomForest(data D, R trees, M features per split):

    FOR r = 1 TO R DO
        D_r   ← bootstrap sample of n instances from D, WITH replacement
        OOB_r ← D \ D_r                    # ≈ 37% of instances, left out
        T_r   ← GrowTree(D_r, M)
    END FOR
    RETURN forest { T_1, ..., T_R }


FUNCTION GrowTree(S, M):

    IF |S| < min_n OR S is pure THEN RETURN Leaf(S)

    F ← M features drawn at random from the P available

    (X*, c*) ← BestSplit(S, searching only over F)   # exactly as in CART

    RETURN Node( split : X* ≤ c* ,
                 left  : GrowTree(S_L, M),
                 right : GrowTree(S_R, M) )
```

::: {style="font-size: 80%"}
The draw of $F$ sits **inside** `GrowTree`, so a fresh set of $M$
features is drawn at *every node* [@breiman2001Random].
:::

## Prediction and the Out-of-Bag Error {.smaller}

``` {.default code-line-numbers="|2-3|6-9|10"}
# Prediction for a new instance x
regression      :  ŷ  =  (1/R) · Σ_r T_r(x)
classification  :  ŷ  =  majority vote over T_1(x), ..., T_R(x)

# Out-of-bag error — a validation set that costs nothing
FOR EACH instance i IN D DO
    S_i  ← { r : i ∈ OOB_r }        # only trees that never saw i
    ŷ_i  ← aggregate { T_r(x_i) : r ∈ S_i }
END FOR
OOB error ← loss(y, ŷ)
```

- Each instance is out-of-bag for roughly $1/e \approx 37\%$ of the
  trees, so every instance gets an honest prediction from about $R/3$ of
  them.
- This is why a random forest can be tuned without a separate validation
  split --- though `tidymodels` will still cross-validate by default.

# Making Predictions

- A tree's prediction uses whatever features happen to appear in its
  split rules.
- Because the candidate set is redrawn at every node, a single tree will
  typically use many more than $M$ features overall.
- The OOB error for instance $i$ aggregates only over the trees for
  which $i$ was out-of-bag.

## Tuning the Random Forest

- $M$, which is called `mtry` in `tidymodels`.
- The number of bootstrap re-samples or trees, $R$, that will be grown;
  `trees` in `tidymodels`.
- The minimal number of observations at the terminal leaves, i.e.,
  `min_n` in `tidymodels`.

## Random Forests in `tidymodels`

::: panel-tabset
### Comment

- Same data, same split, same folds as the CART above --- only the
  algorithm changes.

- We use the `ranger` engine: it is fast, and it samples features **per
  node**, as Breiman intended.

### Model

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
library(ranger)
rf_recipe <- recipe(cmedv ~ ., data = train_data)

rf_spec <- rand_forest(
    mtry  = tune(),
    trees = 500,
    min_n = tune()
  ) |>
  set_mode("regression") |>
  set_engine("ranger", importance = "permutation")

rf_flow <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(rf_recipe) |>
  add_model(rf_spec)
```

### Tuning

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
library(future)
# finalize() is needed because mtry's upper bound depends on the data
rf_param <- extract_parameter_set_dials(rf_spec) |>
  finalize(train_data)

# SMBO-Bayes fine-tuning
plan(multisession)

set.seed(20)
rf_tune <- tune_bayes(
  rf_flow,
  resamples = cv_folds,
  param_info = rf_param,
  initial   = 10,
  iter      = 15,
  metrics   = metric_set(rmse, rsq),
  control   = control_bayes(verbose = TRUE, no_improve = 8)
)
rf_best <- select_best(rf_tune, metric = "rmse")
plan(sequential)
```

### Result
```{r}
rf_best
```

### Final Fit

```{r}
#| echo: true
rf_final <- rf_flow |>
  finalize_workflow(rf_best) |>
  fit(data = train_data)
```

### Performance

```{r}
#| echo: true
rf_final |>
  predict(test_data) |>
  bind_cols(test_data) |>
  metrics(truth = cmedv, estimate = .pred)
```
:::

## A Note on SMBO

- This is the SMBO we promised earlier in the course: each iteration
  fits a surrogate to the results so far and picks the next candidate
  where improvement is most likely.
- `iter = 15` keeps the render honest in class time. For real work you
  would let it run far longer --- and `no_improve` will stop it early if
  the surrogate stops finding anything.
- The surrogate itself is a **Gaussian process**, supplied by the
  `GauPro` package. You do not install it: `tune` depends on it. As of
  `tune` 2.0 it replaced `GPfit`, which is no longer maintained --- so
  the diagnostics printed here differ from older tutorials. Note that
  the surrogate is a *modelling choice*, not a fixed part of the method.

## A Forest of Trees

- There is not a single tree.
- There is now a forest of $R$ trees.
- This helps with performance.
- However, it hampers interpretation.
- But we can get a sense of node importance using `ranger` and
  permutation.

## Which Features Mattered?

::: panel-tabset
### Idea

- A forest has no single tree to read, so we ask a different question:
  **if I destroyed the information in feature** $X_p$, how much worse
  would the predictions get?
- Permutation importance shuffles one feature at a time, re-predicts,
  and records the loss in performance.
- Compare the ranking against the feature your single CART split on
  first.

### Syntax

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
# ranger already computed this, because we set importance = "permutation"
imp <- extract_fit_engine(rf_final)$variable.importance

tibble(feature = names(imp), importance = imp) |>
  slice_max(importance, n = 12) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = importance,
             y = fct_reorder(feature, importance))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#31688EFF") +
  labs(x = "Permutation importance", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
```

### Plot

```{r}
imp <- extract_fit_engine(rf_final)$variable.importance

tibble(feature = names(imp), importance = imp) |>
  slice_max(importance, n = 12) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = importance,
             y = fct_reorder(feature, importance))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#31688EFF") +
  labs(x = "Permutation importance", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
```
:::

Test-set performance on the Boston Housing data, built up as we go:

| Algorithm     | Test RMSE | Test $R^2$ | Notes                               |
|:--------------|:----------|:-----------|:------------------------------------|
| CART          |           |            | one tree, tuned                     |
| Random forest |           |            | bagging + per-node feature sampling |

# adaBoost {background-color="#40666e"}

## adaBoost as an Illustration

-   Introduced by @freund1995DecisionTheoretic.

-   A 2-class classifier that re-weights the data in successive steps.

-   Algorithm

    1.  Start by weighting all training samples equally.

    2.  Fit a tree and record errors.

    3.  Give the falsely predicted samples extra weight.

    4.  Fit another tree.

    5.  Repeat the process.

    6.  Take the predictions from each run and generate weighted predictions, where the weights depend on the quality of the predictions from the individual trees.

## Some Hypothetical Data

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
library(kableExtra)
library(tidyverse)
df <- data.frame( x1 = c(3.648, 2.613, 2.363, 4.933, 3.776, 8.674, 5.862,
                         8.985, 7.467, 4.436),
                  x2 = c(2.997, 4.459, 1.507, 1.299, 3.157, 2.123, 0.004,
                         1.768, 0.187, 0.823),
                  y = c(rep(0, 5), rep(1, 5)) )
df$y <- factor(df$y, labels = c("0", "1"))
df %>% kbl() %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = "striped",
                stripe_color = "gray",
                full_width = F, font_size = 20)
```

## A First Split

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
ggplot(df, aes(x = x1, y = x2, col = y)) +
  geom_point(size = 5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#E69F00", "#56B4E9")) +  # Colorblind-friendly palette
  labs(title = "Scatter Plot of x1 vs x2",
       subtitle = "Colored by Category y with Vertical Line at x1 = 5",
       x = "X1",
       y = "X2",
       color = "Category") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    text = element_text(size = 16), # Larger text for readability
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),  # Center the title
    plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5)
  )
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
-   We make an error for the last instance.

-   The next split should avoid making this error.

-   How do we do this? Through weighting:

    -   Up-weight the incorrectly predicted instance

    -   It now carries more weight in the next learner
:::
:::::

## Weighting Procedure

-   Set the initial weights to $w_i = 1/n_1$ $\forall i$.

-   Apply the algorithm and obtain the prediction errors $m_i \in \{ 0,1 \}$.

-   Obtain the weighted prediction errors

    $$
    e_i = \frac{w_i m_i}{\sum_i w_i}
    $$

-   Define the total error as $e_t = \sum_i e_i$.

-   Define the stage as

    $$
    s = \ln \left( \frac{1 - e_t}{e_t} \right)
    $$

## Weighting Procedure Cont'd

-   Generate updated weights $w_i^* = w_i \exp (s \cdot e_i)$.

-   Move to the next learner and repeat.

## Weighting Illustrated

```{r}
#| echo: false
df$w0 <- 1/10
df$m <- c(rep(0,9), 1)
df$e <- (df$w0 * df$m)/sum(df$w0)
df$e_tot <- sum(df$e)
df$stage <- log((1 - df$e_tot)/df$e_tot)
df$w1 <- df$w0 * exp(df$stage * df$e)
df %>%
  kbl(digits = 3) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = "striped",
                stripe_color = "gray",
                full_width = F,
                font_size = 20)
```

## Fitting Another Stub

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
ggplot(df, aes(x = x1, y = x2, col = y)) +
  geom_point(size = 5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 2.3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#E69F00", "#56B4E9")) +  # Colorblind-friendly palette
  labs(title = "Scatter Plot of x1 vs x2",
       subtitle = "Colored by Category y with Vertical Line at x2 = 2.3",
       x = "X1",
       y = "X2",
       color = "Category") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    text = element_text(size = 16), # Larger text for readability
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),  # Center the title
    plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5)
  )
```
:::

  select(x1,x2,y,w1)
df2$m <- 0
df2[3,5] <- 1
df2[4,5] <- 1
df2$e <- (df2$w1 * df2$m)/sum(df2$w1)
df2$e_tot <- sum(df2$e)
df2$stage <- log((1 - df2$e_tot)/df2$e_tot)
df2$w2 <- df2$w1 * exp(df2$stage * df2$e)
df2 %>%
  kbl(digits = 3) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = "striped", full_width = F,
                font_size = 15)

## And Another One

  select(x1,x2,y,w2)
df3$m <- 0
df3[6,5] <- 1
df3[8,5] <- 1
df3$e <- (df3$w2 * df3$m)/sum(df3$w2)
df3$e_tot <- sum(df3$e)

df3$w3 <- df3$w2 * exp(df3$stage * df3$e)

:::::

## Final Prediction

-   Let $\hat{y}^* = 2\hat{y} - 1$, where $\hat{y} = \{0, 1\}$.

-   For $R$ fitted learners, the prediction for sample $i$ is

    $$
    \hat{y}_i^f = \sum_{r=1}^R s_r \cdot \hat{y}_{ir}^*
    $$

-   If $\hat{y}_i^f \geq 0$ then we predict class label 1, otherwise class label 0.

## Illustration

```{r}
#| echo: false
df4 <- df %>%
  select(x1, x2, y)
df4$psi1 <- ifelse(df4$x1 <= 5, 0, 1)
df4$psi2 <- ifelse(df4$x2 <= 2.3, 1, 0)
df4$psi3 <- ifelse(df4$x2 <= 1, 1, 0)
df4$stage1 <- 2.197
df4$stage2 <- 1.417
df4$stage3 <- 1.452
df4$psi_final <- (2 * df4$psi1 - 1) * df4$stage1 +
  (2 * df4$psi2 - 1) * df4$stage2 +
  (2 * df4$psi3 - 1) * df4$stage3
df4$pred_label <- ifelse(df4$psi_final>=0, 1, 0)
df4 %>%
  kbl(digits = 3) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = "striped", full_width = F,
                font_size = 15)
```

We have achieved perfect prediction.

# Gradient Boosting and XGBoost {background-color="#40666e"}

## What Does a Single Tree Do?

:::::: columns
:::: {.column width="50%"}
![](images/treeboost1.jpg){fig-align="center"}

::: {style="font-size: 75%"}
**Source:** [Distributed Mac hine Learning
Community](https://xgboost.readthedocs.io/en/stable/tutorials/model.html)
:::
::::

::: {.column width="50%"}
- We fit a CART resulting in a prediction $\hat{y}_i$ for the instances.
- This is just the average score in the leaf.
:::
::::::

## How Do We Boost Trees?

:::::: columns
:::: {.column width="50%"}
![](images/treeboost2.jpg){fig-align="center"}

::: {style="font-size: 75%"}
**Source:** [Distributed Mac hine Learning
Community](https://xgboost.readthedocs.io/en/stable/tutorials/model.html)
:::
::::

::: {.column width="50%"}
- A new tree is added to improve predictions.
- Each tree models the residuals (errors) of the previous model.
:::
::::::

## What Are We Optimizing?

- For trees $f_k \in {\cal F}$, where ${\cal F}$ is the set of all
  possible CARTs,
  $$\hat{y}_i = \sum_{k=1}^K f_k(\boldsymbol{x}_i)$$
- The objective function we seek to minimize consists of a loss
  component $L$ and a penalty for complexity [@chen2016XGBoost]:
  $$\text{obj}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} L(y_i,\hat{y}_i) + \sum_{k=1}^K \omega(f_k)$$

## Additive Training

- Boosting builds trees sequentially.
- At step $t$, previous trees $f_1, \dots, f_{t-1}$ are fixed; we only
  optimize the new tree $f_t$:
  $$\text{obj}^{(t)} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} L \left( y_i, \hat{y}_i^{(t-1)} + f_t(\boldsymbol{x}_i) \right) + \omega(f_t) + \text{constant}$$
- Goal: Find $f_t$ that minimizes the overall loss plus tree complexity.

## Sequence of Predictions

1.  Initial prediction $\hat{y}_i^{(0)} = 0$.
2.  At $t=1$,
    $\hat{y}_i^{(1)} = f_1(\boldsymbol{x}_i) = \hat{y}_i^{(0)} + f_1(\boldsymbol{x}_i)$.
3.  At $t=2$,
    $\hat{y}_i^{(2)} = f_1(\boldsymbol{x}_i) + f_2(\boldsymbol{x}_i) = \hat{y}_i^{(1)} + f_2(\boldsymbol{x}_i)$.
4.  Continuing the process, we get
    $$\hat{y}_i^{(t)} = \sum_{k=1}^t f_k (\boldsymbol{x}_i) = \hat{y}_i^{(t-1)} + f_t (\boldsymbol{x}_i)$$

## Example: Exact Quadratic Loss

- If $L(y_i, \hat{y}_i) = (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2$, expanding
  $\text{obj}^{(t)}$ gives:
  $$\begin{align}     \text{Obj}^{(t)} &= \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left( y_i - \left[ \hat{y}_i^{(t-1)} + f_t (\boldsymbol{x}_i) \right] \right)^2 + \omega(f_t) + \text{constant} \\     &= \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[ 2 \underbrace{\left( \hat{y}_i^{(t-1)} - y_i\right)}_{r_i} f_t (\boldsymbol{x}_i) + f_t (\boldsymbol{x}_i)^2 \right] + \omega(f_t) + \text{constant}     \end{align}$$
- **Important:** Note the role of the residual, $r_i$.
- What if $L$ is logistic loss, Huber loss, or a custom loss? We need a
  universal approximation!

## Why Second-Order Taylor Expansion?

- Standard Taylor expansion around base point $x$:
  $$g(x + \Delta x) \approx g(x) + g'(x)\Delta x + \frac{1}{2}g''(x)(\Delta x)^2$$
- Mapping to XGBoost at step $t$:
  - Base point $x$: Current prediction $\hat{y}_i^{(t-1)}$
    (known/fixed).
  - Step $\Delta x$: New tree prediction $f_t(\boldsymbol{x}_i)$ (what
    we solve for).
  - Function $g$: Loss function $L(y_i, \cdot)$.
- Key Benefits:
  - Universal optimization for any smooth loss function!
  - Use of both gradient [@friedman2001Greedy] and Hessian
    [@chen2016XGBoost].

## Applying the Taylor Expansion

- Expanding the loss around $\hat{y}_i^{(t-1)}$:
  $$L\left(y_i, \hat{y}_i^{(t-1)} + f_t(\boldsymbol{x}_i)\right) \approx L\left(y_i, \hat{y}_i^{(t-1)}\right) + g_i f_t(\boldsymbol{x}_i) + \frac{1}{2} h_i f_t^2 (\boldsymbol{x}_i)$$
- Here the first and second derivatives are:
  - Gradient:
    $g_i = \frac{\partial L(y_i, \hat{y}_i^{(t-1)})}{\partial \hat{y}_i^{(t-1)}}$
  - Hessian:
    $h_i = \frac{\partial^2 L(y_i, \hat{y}_i^{(t-1)})}{\partial (\hat{y}_i^{(t-1)})^2}$

## Applying the Taylor Expansion Cont'd

Dropping constants, our objective at step $t$ simplifies to:
$$\text{obj}^{(t)} \approx \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[ g_i f_t(\boldsymbol{x}_i) + \frac{1}{2} h_i f_t^2 (\boldsymbol{x}_i) \right] + \omega(f_t)$$

## What the Expansion Bought Us {.smaller}

This is the payoff. After the expansion, **the loss function has
disappeared**. All that survives of it are two numbers per instance:

$$\text{obj}^{(t)} \approx \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[ \underbrace{g_i}_{\text{one number}} f_t(\boldsymbol{x}_i) + \frac{1}{2} \underbrace{h_i}_{\text{one number}} f_t^2 (\boldsymbol{x}_i) \right] + \omega(f_t)$$

Everything from here on---leaf weights, split gains, the entire
search---touches only $g_i$ and $h_i$. Changing the loss means changing
two formulas and *nothing else*:

::: {style="font-size: 85%"}
| Loss | $L(y_i, \hat{y}_i)$ | $g_i$ | $h_i$ |
|:---------------|:-----------------------|:---------------|:---------------|
| Squared error | $\frac{1}{2}(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2$ | $\hat{y}_i - y_i$ | $1$ |
| Logistic | $\log(1 + e^{\hat{y}_i}) - y_i \hat{y}_i$ | $p_i - y_i$ | $p_i(1 - p_i)$ |
| Poisson | $e^{\hat{y}_i} - y_i \hat{y}_i$ | $e^{\hat{y}_i} - y_i$ | $e^{\hat{y}_i}$ |
:::

::: {style="font-size: 80%"}
where $p_i = 1/(1 + e^{-\hat{y}_i})$. Note squared error gives $h_i = 1$
for every instance---which is exactly why plain gradient boosting, which
ignores $h_i$, works fine for regression and rather less well elsewhere.
:::

::: notes
This is the slide to slow down on. Students who understand that the loss
collapses to (g, h) will follow everything that comes after; students
who do not will experience the rest as unmotivated algebra.
:::

## How to Penalize Over-Fitting?

- Define regularization for a tree $f(x)$:
  $$\omega(f) = \gamma \vert{}T\vert{} + \frac{1}{2} \lambda \sum_{j=1}^{\vert{}T\vert{}} w_j^2$$
- Where:
  - $\vert{}T\vert{}$ is the total number of leaves (penalized by
    $\gamma$).
  - $w_j$ are the leaf output scores (L2 penalized by $\lambda$).
  - Acts like Elastic Net regularization directly on tree structure.

## Structure Score

- Define $f_t(\boldsymbol{x}) = w_{q(\boldsymbol{x})}$, where $w$ are
  leaf scores and $q(\boldsymbol{x})$ assigns instance $i$ to leaf $j$.

- Group instances by leaf $I_j = \{i \mid q(\boldsymbol{x}_i) = j\}$:
  $$\text{Obj}^{(t)} \approx \sum_{j=1}^{\vert{}T\vert{}} \left[ \left( \sum_{i \in I_j} g_i \right) w_j + \frac{1}{2} \left( \sum_{i \in I_j} h_i + \lambda \right) w_j^2 \right] + \gamma \vert{}T\vert{}$$

- Letting $G_j = \sum_{i \in I_j} g_i$ and $H_j = \sum_{i \in I_j} h_i$:
  $$\text{Obj}^{(t)} \approx \sum_{j=1}^{\vert{}T\vert{}} \left[ G_j w_j + \frac{1}{2} (H_j + \lambda) w_j^2 \right] + \gamma\vert{}T\vert{}$$

## Optimums

- Taking derivative w.r.t. $w_j$, the optimal leaf weights are:
  $$w_j^* = - \frac{G_j}{H_j + \lambda}$$

- Substituting $w_j^*$ back gives the optimal objective (Structure
  Score):
  $$\text{Obj}^* = -\frac{1}{2} \sum_{j=1}^{\vert{}T\vert{}} \frac{G_j^2}{H_j + \lambda} + \gamma\vert{}T\vert{}$$

- $\text{Obj}^*$ measures how "good" a given tree structure is (smaller
  is better).
  
## Visualizing Tree Quality

![](images/treeboost3.png){fig-align="center"}

## Reading the Structure Score {.smaller}

Look at what $\text{Obj}^*$ actually is---**a sum of one term per
leaf**:
$$\text{Obj}^* = \sum_{j=1}^{\lvert T \rvert} \left[ \underbrace{-\frac{1}{2}\frac{G_j^2}{H_j + \lambda}}_{\text{what leaf } j \text{ contributes}} + \underbrace{\gamma}_{\text{what leaf } j \text{ costs}} \right]$$
Call $s_j = \dfrac{G_j^2}{H_j + \lambda}$ the [**leaf score**]{.alert}. A good tree has large total leaf score and few
leaves.

-   $s_j$ is large when the gradients in the leaf **agree** (big $\lvert G_j \rvert$): the instances in that leaf all want the prediction moved the same way.

-   $s_j$ is small when they cancel out ($G_j \approx 0$): the leaf has nothing useful to say, whatever its size.

## From Score to Split {.smaller}

Take one leaf, currently holding all its instances, and consider cutting it in two.

::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
**Before the split** --- one leaf, score $s_P$, cost $\gamma$:
$$
s_P = \frac{(G_L + G_R)^2}{H_L + H_R + \lambda}
$$

**After the split** --- two leaves, cost $2\gamma$:

$$
s_L + s_R = \frac{G_L^2}{H_L + \lambda} + \frac{G_R^2}{H_R + \lambda}
$$
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
Nothing else in the tree changes, so the improvement is just the difference:

$$\text{IG} = \frac{1}{2}\left[ s_L + s_R - s_P \right] - \gamma$$

which is exactly the formula on the next slide. The three terms are not arbitrary: **left child, right child, and the parent they replace.**
:::
:::::

::: {style="font-size: 85%"}
$G_P = G_L + G_R$ and $H_P = H_L + H_R$ because the instances are merely being re-partitioned---none are created or destroyed. And $\gamma$ is now readable: it is the *entrance fee* for one extra leaf. If splitting does not buy at least $\gamma$ worth of score, do not split.
:::


## Reading the Structure Score Cont'd

::: callout-important
Because $\text{Obj}^*$ is a *sum over leaves*, changing one leaf changes
**only that leaf's term**. Every other leaf is untouched. This is what
makes a local, greedy search legitimate---and it is the entire reason
the next slide works.
:::

# Choosing the Feature and the Cut-Point {.smaller}

There is **no separate feature-selection step**. The feature is simply whichever one wins the argmax.

```{.default code-line-numbers="|3|6|7|8|10|11|12|14|16|19"}
FUNCTION BestSplit(leaf I):

    G ← Σ_{i∈I} g_i ;  H ← Σ_{i∈I} h_i        # totals for this leaf
    best ← (feature: none, point: none, gain: 0)

    FOR EACH feature X_p DO
        sort the instances of I by x_ip
        G_L ← 0 ; H_L ← 0                     # left child starts empty

        FOR EACH instance i IN sorted order DO
            G_L ← G_L + g_i ; H_L ← H_L + h_i     # move i to the left
            G_R ← G − G_L   ; H_R ← H − H_L       # right child, for free

            IG ← ½[ G_L²/(H_L+λ) + G_R²/(H_R+λ) − G²/(H+λ) ] − γ

            IF IG > best.gain THEN best ← (X_p, x_ip, IG)
        END FOR
    END FOR
    RETURN best        # best.gain ≤ 0  ⇒  make this a leaf, do not split
```

::: {style="font-size: 80%"}
Identical in shape to the CART search---only the scoring function has changed. A feature "enters the model" precisely when some cut-point on it wins line 16 somewhere in some tree.
:::

## Splitting on Features

-   Gain from splitting a leaf into Left ($L$) and Right ($R$) branches:
    $$
    \text{IG} = \frac{1}{2} \left[ \frac{G_L^2}{H_L + \lambda} + \frac{G_R^2}{H_R + \lambda} - \frac{\left( G_L + G_R \right)^2}{H_L + H_R + \lambda} \right] - \gamma
    $$
-   $\gamma$ acts as a threshold: if $\text{IG} < 0$ (i.e. gain $< \gamma$), the split is pruned.

## Why the Scan Is Cheap {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
The naive way to evaluate a cut-point is to add up the gradients on each side from scratch. With $n$ instances and $n$ candidate cut-points, that is $n$ additions done $n$ times.

The trick: sort once, then sweep the cut-point from left to right. Each step moves **exactly one instance** from the right child to the left:

$$G_L \leftarrow G_L + g_i \qquad G_R = G - G_L$$

$$H_L \leftarrow H_L + h_i \qquad H_R = H - H_L$$

Nothing is ever re-summed. The right child comes for free by subtraction, because the two children must add up to the parent.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: callout-note
## The idea in one line

Don't recompute the sum---**update** it [@chen2016XGBoost].
:::

So evaluating each additional cut-point costs a *constant* amount of work, no matter how many instances are in the leaf.

This is the same running-sums idea that made the CART scan cheap. Here it matters more, because it happens once per leaf, per feature, per tree, for hundreds of trees.
:::
:::::

## Cost, for Reference {.smaller visibility="uncounted"}

::: {style="font-size: 90%"}
| Method | Cost per feature, per leaf | Idea |
|:------------------|:------------------|:---------------------------------|
| Naive re-summing | $O(n^2)$ | recompute both sides at every cut-point |
| Exact greedy | $O(n \log n)$ sort, then $O(n)$ sweep | sort once, update running sums |
| Histogram (`tree_method = "hist"`) | $O(B)$ with $B \approx 256$ | pre-bin the feature; scan buckets, not instances |
:::

-   The histogram method is why XGBoost and LightGBM scale to millions of rows: the sweep no longer depends on $n$ at all, only on the number of buckets.

-   The bins are built once, from quantiles of the feature, and reused for every tree.

::: notes
Marked `visibility="uncounted"` so it does not consume a slide number — treat it as a reference slide to skip or linger on depending on the room.
:::

## Hyper-parameter Taxonomy and Math Mapping

| Parameter | Symbol | Role | Impact/Guidance                              |
|:--------------------|:----|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|
|`learn_rate`|$\eta$|Step-size shrinkage|Small (0.01–0.1) prevents overfitting|
|`tree_depth`|---|Max tree depth|Keep low (3–7) to limit interactions|
|`min_n`|$\sum h_i$|Min sum of Hessians|Prevents fitting noise in small leaves|
|`loss_reduction`|$\gamma$|Split threshold|Minimum gain required to split|
|`reg_lambda`|$\lambda$|L2 leaf score penalty|Higher values shrink weights $w_j^*$|
|`sample_size`/`mtry`|---|Subsampling ratios|Adds randomness (bagging / RF style)|

## Tree-Specific Parameters

- `tree_depth`: Maximum depth of a tree (controls model complexity).
- `sample_size`: Subsample ratio of training instances.
- `mtry`: Subsample ratio of columns when constructing each tree.
- `min_n`: Minimum sum of instance weight (Hessian) needed in a child.

## General and Regularization Parameters

- `learn_rate` ($\eta$): Scales individual tree contributions: $\hat{y}^{(t)} = \hat{y}^{(t-1)} + \eta f_t(\boldsymbol{x})$.
- `trees` (nrounds): Total number of boosting iterations.
- `loss_reduction` ($\gamma$) & reg_lambda ($\lambda$): Tree structure penalties.

## XGBoost Workflow for the Boston Housing Data

::: panel-tabset
### Comment
We keep everything from nthe previous modles we ran.

### Recipe

```{r}
#| echo: true
xgb_recipe <- recipe(cmedv ~ ., data = train_data) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())
```

### Specification

```{r}
#| echo: true
xgb_spec <- boost_tree(
  trees          = 500,
  tree_depth     = tune(),
  min_n          = tune(),
  loss_reduction = tune(),
  sample_size    = tune(),
  mtry           = tune(),
  learn_rate     = tune()
) |>
  set_engine("xgboost") |>
  set_mode("regression")
```

### Flow

```{r}
#| echo: true
xgb_flow <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(xgb_recipe) |>
  add_model(xgb_spec)
```
:::

## Tuning with Bayesian Optimization

::: panel-tabset
### Syntax

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
xgb_param <- extract_parameter_set_dials(xgb_spec) |>
  finalize(train_data)

library(future)
plan(multisession)                 
set.seed(123)
xgb_tune <- tune_bayes(
  xgb_flow,
  resamples = cv_folds,
  param_info = xgb_param,
  initial   = 10,
  iter      = 15,
  metrics   = metric_set(rmse, rsq),
  control   = control_bayes(verbose = TRUE, no_improve = 8)
)
xgb_best <- select_best(xgb_tune, metric = "rmse")
plan(sequential)                   # release the workers
xgb_best
```

### Progress

```{r}
#| echo: true
autoplot(xgb_tune, type = "performance")
```
:::

## Final Fit and Performance

::: panel-tabset
### Finalize

```{r}
#| echo: true
xgb_final <- xgb_flow |>
  finalize_workflow(xgb_best) |>
  fit(data = train_data)
```

### Test Set

```{r}
#| echo: true
xgb_final |>
  predict(test_data) |>
  bind_cols(test_data) |>
  metrics(truth = cmedv, estimate = .pred)
```

### Predicted vs Actual

```{r}
#| echo: true
xgb_final |>
  predict(test_data) |>
  bind_cols(test_data) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = cmedv, y = .pred)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, colour = "#31688EFF") +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Actual", y = "Predicted") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
```
:::
